Mohsen Rezaei's negotiating calculus: someone else always pays the price
Author: Mahdi Amiri | Iran International | November 2, 2026
(Extracted summary of article text)
The analysis examines how Mohsen Rezaei, now Iran's top security official, has historically made consequential decisions while insulating himself and allies from the consequences—a pattern that shapes his negotiating approach with Washington.
Rezaei's career as IRGC commander during the Iran-Iraq War: when Iraq offered negotiations after recapturing Khorramshahr in 1982, Rezaei advocated continuing the conflict, ultimately extending the war six additional years.
The article contends that "economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing."
Post-war positions—from Expediency Council secretary to economic policy roles—enabled Rezaei to maintain influence while ordinary Iranians absorbed economic costs.
The analysis suggests pressure targeting Iranian households alone may prove insufficient; meaningful negotiations require decision-makers themselves to face credible personal costs for renewed confrontation.
